topic: Weimar Germany (y9 history), smoke r7 design-cycle.v5

objectives.text: Explain how reparations, the Ruhr occupation and passive resistance led to hyperinflation

arc.angle: How the government's response to the Ruhr occupation increased the money supply and prices
arc.misconception: Printing more money made Germany richer

objectives.text: Explain how hyperinflation affected the savings, wages and daily lives of different groups

arc.angle: Why people on fixed incomes and people with debts experienced the crisis differently
arc.misconception: Everyone in Germany was affected in the same way

retrieval.question: What is a currency?
retrieval.answer: The money used in a country

retrieval.question: What is the difference between income and savings?
retrieval.answer: Income is money received; savings are money kept for later

retrieval.question: What does it mean to borrow money?
retrieval.answer: To receive money now and agree to repay it later

slots.notes: Explain that the Ruhr was an important industrial region, producing coal and other goods. France and Belgium occupied it in January 1923 after Germany fell behind on reparations payments. Reparations were payments Germany had been required to make after the First World War.
slots.heading: French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr
slots.body: The occupation took control of a major industrial region of Germany. It followed Germany’s failure to keep up with reparations payments.

imageBrief.subject: Archival photograph of French or Belgian troops in the Ruhr during its 1923 occupation
mustShow: Troops in a street or near industrial buildings
A recognisable historical setting from the early 1920s

slots.notes: Trace the chain aloud: reparations payments were due; the Ruhr was occupied; German workers resisted by refusing to work; the government supported them by paying their wages despite lost production; it created money to meet these costs. With fewer goods being produced and more money circulating, prices rose rapidly. This is hyperinflation: an extremely fast rise in prices. Printing money did not create more goods or make the country richer.
slots.heading: Paying striking workers helped drive prices up
slots.body: The government paid workers who resisted the Ruhr occupation, even though less was being produced, and printed money to cover the cost.

callout.text: Printing more money did not make Germany richer. More money chased fewer goods, so prices rose rapidly.

slots.notes: Ask pupils to choose an answer independently, then discuss why the other options are tempting but wrong. Look for the link between passive resistance, government spending, money supply and prices.
slots.stem: Why did the government’s response to passive resistance help cause hyperinflation?

options.text: It printed money to pay workers while production fell, so prices rose
It printed money that increased the amount of goods available
It stopped reparations payments, so prices immediately fell
It made Ruhr workers produce more goods, so money became scarce

slots.explanation: The government created money to pay workers who were not producing goods, increasing the money supply as the supply of goods fell.

exitQuestion.question: How did paying workers during passive resistance contribute to hyperinflation?
exitQuestion.answer: The government printed money to pay workers while production fell, so more money chased fewer goods and prices rose.

slots.notes: Explain that a fixed income is money that stays the same, such as a pension or a salary that has not yet been adjusted. As prices rose quickly, the same amount of money bought less. People with debts could sometimes repay them with money that had lost much of its value, although this did not help everyone with debts equally.
slots.heading: Fixed incomes lost value, while some debts became easier to repay
slots.body: Rapid price rises affected people differently, depending on their income and debts.

right.label: People with debts
points: Could repay loans with less valuable money
Some debts became easier to clear

slots.notes: Ask pupils what they notice about the money and the shop goods. Explain that prices could change so quickly that wages or savings did not keep up. Avoid suggesting that every household had the same experience: the effects depended on a person’s income, savings and debts.
slots.heading: Daily shopping became difficult as prices soared
slots.body: People needed more and more marks to buy everyday goods. Those paid at a fixed rate could find that their money no longer covered basic needs.

imageBrief.subject: A historical-style scene of a person shopping in Germany during the 1923 hyperinflation crisis
mustShow: A customer holding a large bundle of banknotes
A small selection of everyday goods in a shop
No legible modern packaging or identifiable people

slots.notes: Pupils should reject the idea that everyone experienced hyperinflation in the same way. Ask them to explain why the two groups differed: prices rose rapidly, but fixed incomes did not keep pace, while some borrowers could repay debts in money worth less than when they borrowed it.
slots.stem: Why could hyperinflation affect a pensioner and a person with a loan differently?

options.text: A pension could lose buying power, while some debts became easier to repay
Both always gained because everyone received more banknotes
Both were affected in exactly the same way
A pension rose automatically whenever prices rose

slots.explanation: Prices rose faster than many fixed incomes, while some borrowers could repay loans with money that had lost value.

exitQuestion.question: Why could hyperinflation harm someone on a fixed income but help someone with a debt?
exitQuestion.answer: A fixed income bought less as prices rose, while some debts could be repaid with money that had lost value.

electrolysisWorkedExample.notes: Read the question carefully for both the ions present and whether the solution is concentrated. At the anode, negative ions lose electrons. In this example, concentrated chloride ions form chlorine rather than hydroxide ions forming oxygen.
electrolysisWorkedExample.heading: Predicting the anode product in concentrated sodium chloride
electrolysisWorkedExample.question: What forms at the anode during electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride?
steps: The solution contains chloride ions and hydroxide ions.
Because the solution is concentrated, chloride ions form the halogen at the anode.
Chlorine gas forms at the anode.

buyingPowerWorkedExample.notes: Work through the two prices with the class. Buying power means how much a sum of money can purchase. Emphasise that the number of marks stays the same, but the money buys fewer loaves when prices rise. This is an invented example, not a claim about the actual price of bread in Germany.
buyingPowerWorkedExample.heading: Comparing what savings and wages could buy
buyingPowerWorkedExample.question: A worker has 100 marks in savings and earns 10 marks in a day. A loaf rises in price from 1 mark to 10 marks. How does this change what the money can buy?
steps: At 1 mark per loaf, 100 marks buys 100 loaves; 10 marks of daily pay buys 10 loaves.
At 10 marks per loaf, the same 100 marks buys 10 loaves; 10 marks of daily pay buys 1 loaf.
The savings’ buying power falls from 100 loaves to 10, and the daily pay’s falls from 10 loaves to 1.
